section.title: Cities of Refuge
section.sectionRationale: As the tribes prepare to settle their allotted land, God provides for the Levites, who receive no territory of their own, and establishes six cities of refuge where someone who kills unintentionally can flee from the avenger of blood. This law holds together real justice for murder and real mercy for the unintentional, a pattern later Scripture reads as a picture of refuge found in Christ.
section.thesis: The Levites receive forty-eight cities with pasturelands instead of tribal territory, six of which are set apart as cities of refuge where a person who kills someone unintentionally may flee for protection from the avenger of blood, safe there until the death of the high priest, while a deliberate murderer finds no such shelter and must be put to death.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the Levites given cities and pasturelands instead of land; six of those cities set apart as places of refuge; the sharp legal distinction between murder and unintentional killing; and the rules of testimony, ransom, and bloodguilt that protect the land's holiness.

verses.text: Again the LORD spoke to Moses on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho:
“Command the Israelites to give, from the inheritance they will possess, cities for the Levites to live in and pasturelands around the cities.
The cities will be for them to live in, and the pasturelands will be for their herds, their flocks, and all their other livestock.
The pasturelands around the cities you are to give the Levites will extend a thousand cubits from the wall on every side.

You are also to measure two thousand cubits outside the city on the east, two thousand on the south, two thousand on the west, and two thousand on the north, with the city in the center. These areas will serve as larger pasturelands for the cities.
Six of the cities you give the Levites are to be appointed as cities of {{refuge|refuge}}, to which a manslayer may flee. In addition to these, give the Levites forty-two other cities.
The total number of cities you give the Levites will be forty-eight, with their corresponding pasturelands.

The cities that you apportion from the territory of the Israelites should be given to the Levites in proportion to the inheritance of each tribe: more from a larger tribe and less from a smaller one.”

media.alt: A city gate standing open on a hillside road as evening falls
media.caption: A refuge from the avenger, until the death of the high priest.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan,
designate cities to serve as your cities of refuge, so that a person who kills someone unintentionally may flee there.
You are to have these cities as a refuge from the {{avenger|avenger of blood}}, so that the manslayer will not die until he stands trial before the assembly.
The cities you select will be your six cities of refuge.
Select three cities across the Jordan and three in the land of Canaan as cities of refuge.
These six cities will serve as a refuge for the Israelites and for the foreigner or stranger among them, so that anyone who kills a person unintentionally may flee there.

units.label: Murder distinguished from manslaughter
units.note: the murderer must surely be put to death

verses.text: If, however, anyone strikes a person with an iron object and kills him, he is a murderer; the murderer must surely be put to death.
Or if anyone has in his hand a stone of deadly size, and he strikes and kills another, he is a murderer; the murderer must surely be put to death.
If anyone has in his hand a deadly object of wood, and he strikes and kills another, he is a murderer; the murderer must surely be put to death.
The avenger of blood is to put the murderer to death; when he finds him, he is to kill him.
Likewise, if anyone maliciously pushes another or intentionally throws an object at him and kills him,
or if in hostility he strikes him with his hand and he dies, the one who struck him must surely be put to death; he is a murderer. When the avenger of blood finds the murderer, he is to kill him.
But if anyone pushes a person suddenly, without hostility, or throws an object at him unintentionally,
or without looking drops a heavy stone that kills him, but he was not an enemy and did not intend to harm him,
then the congregation must judge between the slayer and the avenger of blood according to these ordinances.

The assembly is to protect the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood. Then the assembly will return him to the city of refuge to which he fled, and he must live there until the death of the high priest, who was anointed with the holy oil.

units.label: Testimony, ransom, and the holiness of the land

verses.text: But if the manslayer ever goes outside the limits of the city of refuge to which he fled
and the avenger of blood finds him outside of his city of refuge and kills him, then the avenger will not be guilty of bloodshed
because the manslayer must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest. Only after the death of the high priest may he return to the land he owns.
This will be a statutory ordinance for you for the generations to come, wherever you live.
If anyone kills a person, the murderer is to be put to death on the testimony of the witnesses. But no one is to be put to death based on the testimony of a lone witness.
You are not to accept a ransom for the life of a murderer who deserves to die; he must surely be put to death.
Nor should you accept a ransom for the person who flees to a city of refuge and allow him to return and live on his own land before the death of the high priest.
Do not pollute the land where you live, for bloodshed pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land on which the blood is shed, except by the blood of the one who shed it.
Do not defile the land where you live and where I dwell. For I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites.”

refuge.gloss: Refuge, a place of shelter. A miqlat city was not a hiding place from justice but a place of due process, protecting the unintentional killer from vengeance until a fair trial determined guilt, a real, physical picture of Scripture's larger theme of finding refuge from deserved judgment in God Himself.

avenger.gloss: Avenger of blood, literally kinsman-redeemer of blood, the near relative responsible for pursuing justice for a slain family member. The same word, go'el, is elsewhere used positively of a redeemer who buys back a relative's loss, showing that justice and redemption in Hebrew thought were carried by kin rather than distant institutions alone.

basic.context: The Levites, who receive no tribal territory of their own, are given forty-eight cities scattered throughout the land, six of which are set apart as cities of refuge. Anyone who kills another person unintentionally can flee there for protection from the victim's avenging relative, safe until a fair trial, and safe within the city's borders until the current high priest dies. A deliberate murderer, by contrast, finds no such shelter.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real, practical law establishing due process and mercy within Israel's justice system, carefully distinguishing between murder and accident. Its precision, defining weapons, intent, and witnesses, shows a legal system determined to protect both true justice for murder and genuine mercy for those who kill without intending harm.
basic.originalLanguages: A miqlat, city of refuge, was not an escape from justice but a place where due process could unfold safely, protecting a person from the go'el hadam, avenger of blood, until guilt or innocence was properly established. The same root go'el elsewhere describes a kinsman-redeemer who buys back what was lost, linking blood justice and redemption to the same family responsibility.
basic.typology: The cities of refuge, offering real safety from deserved judgment to anyone who reaches them, and holding that safety only until the death of the high priest, are widely read as a picture of refuge found in Christ, our great High Priest, whose own death secures permanent freedom for all who flee to Him, Hebrews 6:18.
basic.christ: Hebrews 6:18 speaks of believers who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before them, language many read as directly echoing this very institution; and where the manslayer's freedom in these ancient cities came only through the death of an earthly high priest, believers' freedom comes through the death of Jesus, our eternal High Priest, whose one sacrifice secures release once for all.
basic.god: God is both perfectly just, requiring the death penalty for deliberate murder and refusing any ransom to buy off that judgment, and perfectly merciful, providing real, accessible, physical shelter for those who kill without murderous intent. His holiness will not let the land bear unaddressed bloodguilt, yet His compassion ensures the innocent are not swept away with the guilty.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 19:1-13 and Joshua 20 give further instructions and the actual naming of these six cities. Hebrews 6:18 describes believers fleeing for refuge to the hope set before them, language closely echoing this institution. Proverbs 18:10 pictures the name of the LORD as a strong tower where the righteous run and are safe.
basic.oneStory: Real justice for the guilty and real mercy for the innocent are held together in this law rather than set against each other. That same combination, holy justice and genuine refuge, runs through the whole Bible and finds its fullest expression in Christ, the true and eternal High Priest, whose death secures permanent, unshakeable safety for everyone who flees to Him in faith.

context.literary:
Numbers 35 is set, like the chapters around it, 'on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho,' verse 1, and it holds two speeches. The first, verses 1 to 8, gives the Levites cities and pasturelands. The second, verses 9 to 34, sets six of those cities apart for refuge and lays down the law of homicide that governs them. The two are joined by verse 6: the cities of refuge are Levitical cities.

The legal section is carefully built. It moves from the purpose of the cities, verses 9 to 15, to the definition of murder, verses 16 to 21, to the definition of unintentional killing, verses 22 to 24, to the procedure, verses 24 to 28, and finally to general principles, verses 29 to 34. The murder cases are shaped by repetition. Three times, for an iron object, a stone and a wooden object, the text concludes, 'he is a murderer; the murderer must surely be put to death,' verses 16 to 18. Then the tests shift from the weapon to the heart: hatred, lying in wait, hostility, verses 20 and 21. Against these stand three mirror cases of pushing, throwing and dropping 'without hostility' or 'without looking,' verses 22 and 23. The structure itself teaches that the question is intent, not merely outcome.

The chapter ends on theology rather than procedure. Verses 33 and 34 give the reason behind all the rules: bloodshed pollutes the land, only the blood of the killer atones for it, and the land must not be defiled because 'I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites.' Law that began with city plans ends with the presence of God.

Within the book's closing section, the chapter follows the division of the land in chapter 34 and precedes the protection of inheritances in chapter 36. Before the tribes receive their land, God ensures that the land will have room for those who serve at His altar and shelter for those who might otherwise be swept away by vengeance.
context.historical:
The Levites had been set apart in place of Israel's firstborn, Numbers 3:12, and were given no tribal territory, for 'I am your portion and your inheritance,' Numbers 18:20. Forty-eight cities, roughly four from each tribe, spread them through the land, Joshua 21:41. Jacob's dying words had said of Simeon and Levi, 'I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel,' Genesis 49:7. In Levi's case, after their zeal at Sinai, Exodus 32:26-29, the scattering became a ministry: teachers of the law living in every region.

In much of the ancient world, justice for a killing was pursued by the victim's family. The go'el haddam, the avenger of blood, was the nearest kinsman, charged with seeing that a death was answered. Such a system protected families where there was no police force, but it could easily run hot. Deuteronomy 19:6 names the danger: the avenger might pursue 'in a rage' and kill someone 'though he did not deserve to die.' The story of the woman of Tekoa, 2 Samuel 14:11, shows how real the fear of the avenger remained under the monarchy.

Other ancient peoples knew sanctuary at temples and altars, and Israel had that too. Exodus 21:13-14 promised 'a place where he may flee' and denied the altar's protection to the deliberate killer. Adonijah and Joab both grasped the horns of the altar, 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28. What is distinctive in Numbers 35 is that refuge becomes a network of cities placed across the whole land, three on each side of the Jordan, verse 14, later named in Joshua 20:7-8: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron in the west; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead and Golan in the east. Deuteronomy 19:3 even requires roads to be built to them.

The protection was open to 'the foreigner or stranger among them,' verse 15. The pasturelands, a thousand cubits from the wall, roughly 450 metres in the BSB footnote, gave the Levites room for flocks and herds.
context.canonical:
The concern of this chapter reaches back to the beginning. The first murder ends with God saying, 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground,' Genesis 4:10, and after the flood God declares, 'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind,' Genesis 9:6. Exodus 21:12-14 first promised a place of flight for the unintentional killer. Numbers 35 builds that promise into the life of the land.

Deuteronomy 4:41-43 records Moses setting apart the three eastern cities, and Deuteronomy 19:1-13 repeats the law with added provisions, roads and the prospect of more cities if the land grew. Joshua 20 carries it out, adding that the manslayer states his case at the city gate before the elders, Joshua 20:4. Deuteronomy 21:1-9 addresses the unsolved murder, where the elders must make atonement so that innocent blood does not remain on the land.

The warning of verse 33 proves prophetic. Psalm 106:38 says Israel shed innocent blood, 'and the land was polluted with blood.' 2 Kings 24:3-4 names the innocent blood shed by Manasseh as a reason for Judah's exile. The land did what Leviticus 18:28 had warned and cast its people out.

The Psalms and prophets take up the language of refuge and apply it to God Himself: 'God is our refuge and strength,' Psalm 46:1; 'You have been a refuge for the poor,' Isaiah 25:4. In the New Testament, Hebrews 6:18 speaks of believers 'who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' language that sounds like the flight to a city of refuge. The rule of verse 30 that no one is condemned on one witness is repeated by Jesus in Matthew 18:16 and by Paul in 2 Corinthians 13:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to grasp that human life belongs to God and that its taking must be answered, and at the same time that justice must be just. The chapter refuses both easy solutions. It does not let a murderer buy his way out, verse 31, and it does not let grief or rage kill a man who never intended harm, verses 22 to 25. Every killing is serious; not every killing is murder.

The first hearers were also meant to see that justice is a community responsibility. The assembly judges between the slayer and the avenger, verse 24; witnesses are required, verse 30; the Levites, who teach the law, host the refuge. Vengeance is no longer a private family matter but is placed under the judgment of the congregation and the law of God.

Above all, the chapter ties justice to worship. The land is where God dwells, verse 34. Unanswered bloodshed defiles it and endangers Israel's life in it. By keeping this law Israel would keep the land fit for the presence of the LORD. Obedience here was not only good civic order; it was a way of honouring the holy God who had chosen to live among them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The cities of refuge were a specific institution for Israel's tribal society in the land, and the New Testament does not ask the church to build them or to adopt the avenger of blood. Modern states administer justice through courts, and Romans 13:4 gives the governing authority the sword.

What carries forward is the moral structure of the law. Life is sacred because humanity bears God's image, Genesis 9:6. Intent matters to guilt, and Jesus presses that further, teaching that anger and contempt stand under judgment, Matthew 5:21-22. Due process matters: no one is condemned on a lone witness, verse 30, a principle the church still uses in discipline, Matthew 18:16. Justice cannot be bought by the powerful, verse 31. And the innocent must be protected from rage.

The chapter also prescribes a pattern of refuge that the gospel fulfils rather than replaces. The one who flees to Christ is safe, not because justice has been ignored, but because it has been satisfied.

debates.question: Why does the manslayer's release depend on the death of the high priest?

views.label: The high priest's death had an atoning, releasing effect
views.case: The high priest represented the whole nation before God and was 'anointed with the holy oil,' verse 25. Since verse 33 insists that blood defiles the land and needs atonement, the death of the anointed priest may have been treated as closing the matter for the community. Later Jewish interpreters read it this way, and it explains why verse 32 forbids a ransom to shorten the term.

views.label: It marked an impartial, national turning point
views.case: The death of a high priest ended an era. Tying release to it gave an endpoint that neither the manslayer nor the avenger could control or predict, much as an amnesty might attend a change of reign. On this view the rule is about public order and cooling of passions rather than atonement.

views.label: It was a real penalty that stopped short of death
views.case: The manslayer was not blameless. A life had been lost through his hands, and his exile from his own land was a genuine consequence, bounded by the life of the priest so that it was neither endless nor trivial.

debates.bearing: The views overlap. The manslayer's confinement was a real consequence, and his release came through a priestly death rather than through merit or the passage of time. That is why Christians have long seen here a pointer to the release secured by the death of Jesus, the high priest who, unlike Aaron's sons, lives forever, Hebrews 7:23-25.

debates.question: How do the thousand cubits of verse 4 fit with the two thousand cubits of verse 5?

views.label: Two zones of pastureland
views.case: Verse 4 measures a thousand cubits outward from the wall, and verse 5 speaks of 'larger pasturelands' two thousand cubits on each side. On this reading an inner belt served for livestock and an outer belt for fields or further grazing.

views.label: A square two thousand cubits on each side
views.case: Others take verse 5 as measuring a square whose sides are two thousand cubits long, with the city in the centre. If the city is small, the distance from wall to edge is about a thousand cubits, so the two verses describe one area in two ways.

debates.bearing: The details remain uncertain, but the purpose is clear. The Levites were given real, measured land for their livelihood, not a vague right to live on others' charity.

study.originalLanguages:
The noun behind 'manslayer' in verses 6, 11 and 12 and 'murderer' in verses 16 to 21 is the same: rotseach, from ratsach, the verb of the sixth commandment, 'You shall not murder,' Exodus 20:13. Hebrew uses one word for the one who kills, and the context decides whether the killing was murder. That is why the chapter needs so many qualifying phrases. The commandment's verb covers the act; the law of refuge weighs the heart.

The key qualifier is bishgagah, 'unintentionally,' verses 11 and 15. Shegagah is the word for unintentional sin in the laws of the sin offering, 'one who sins unintentionally,' Leviticus 4:2 and Numbers 15:27-28. Unintentional sin is still sin and still needs atonement, but it is set against sin done 'defiantly,' Numbers 15:30, for which no offering avails. The manslayer belongs to the first category, the murderer to the second.

The tests of intent are precise. Verse 20 speaks of pushing 'maliciously,' literally in hatred, and of throwing 'intentionally,' with a word that means lying in wait, the same idea as Exodus 21:13, 'if he did not lie in wait.' Verses 21 and 22 turn on eivah, hostility or enmity, with it or 'without hostility.' It is the word of Genesis 3:15, 'I will put enmity between you and the woman.' The law of murder is concerned with the enmity that has entered human hearts since the fall.

Go'el haddam, 'the avenger of blood,' uses go'el, the kinsman who acts on behalf of the family. The same word describes the redeemer who buys back a relative's land, Leviticus 25:25, Boaz as kinsman-redeemer, Ruth 4:14, and the LORD Himself: 'Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel,' Isaiah 41:14. The go'el is the one who puts things right for the family, whether by redemption or by retribution.

Kopher, 'ransom,' in verses 31 and 32, belongs to the same root as kipper, 'to make atonement,' in verse 33. The chapter deliberately places them side by side: no ransom may be taken for a murderer's life, and no atonement can be made for polluted land except by the blood of the one who shed it. Psalm 49:7 uses kopher when it says no man can pay God a ransom for his brother. Exodus 21:30 shows that in some cases a ransom was permitted, which makes the refusal here more pointed.

Finally, verses 33 and 34 use two verbs of defilement, chanaph, to pollute, and tame, to make unclean, and close with shakan, to dwell, twice: 'the land where you live and where I dwell,' and 'I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites.' Shakan is the root of mishkan, the tabernacle. Murder is not only a crime against a neighbour; it pollutes the ground on which God has pitched His tent.

typology.type: Cities of refuge open to anyone who flees there
typology.fulfillment: The cities offered shelter to Israelite, foreigner and stranger alike, verse 15, provided they fled and stayed within the walls. Hebrews 6:18 describes believers as those 'who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' and Paul's great aim is to 'be found in Him,' Philippians 3:9, just as the manslayer had to be found inside the city. The escalation is that Christ is a refuge for the guilty as well as the unintentional, and 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1. The type falls short because the cities protected only from the avenger, not from God's judgment.

typology.type: Release through the death of the high priest
typology.fulfillment: The manslayer could go home only after the high priest who was 'anointed with the holy oil' died, verses 25 and 28. Hebrews says that earlier priests were many because 'death prevented them from continuing in office,' but Jesus 'lives forever' and 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:23-25. His one death secured 'eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12. The correspondence is strong, and the escalation is that the release He gives never needs repeating. The type falls short because Israel's high priest did not choose to die for the manslayer; Christ gave Himself deliberately.

typology.type: The go'el, kinsman who acts for the family
typology.fulfillment: The avenger of blood was the near relative who answered for a slain family member, and the same word names the kinsman-redeemer. Christ became our kinsman by sharing our flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, and He is the Redeemer Job longed for, Job 19:25. In Him the two sides of the go'el meet: He redeems His people, and He will one day avenge the blood of His servants, Revelation 19:2. The type falls short because a human avenger could act in rage and error; Christ's judgment is true and just.

typology.type: Blood that atones for polluted land
typology.fulfillment: Verse 33 says that land defiled by bloodshed is atoned for only by the blood of the one who shed it. The gospel reverses the direction without cancelling the principle. Jesus, who shed no one's blood, gave His own. His 'sprinkled blood' 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel,' Hebrews 12:24, which once cried from the ground, and 'the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin,' 1 John 1:7. The type falls short because the blood of a murderer only answered a crime; Christ's blood reconciles the guilty to God.

study.christ:
The cities of refuge lead to Christ by pattern, and the New Testament itself points the way. Hebrews 6:18 describes believers as those 'who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' and the next verses speak of that hope as an anchor that 'enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain,' 'where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever,' Hebrews 6:19-20. The flight, the refuge and the high priest all appear in the same breath.

The heart of the connection is the high priest's death. Under this law a person could be safe in the city and still not free; only the death of the anointed high priest let him go home, verse 28. Jesus is the anointed one, and His death is the event on which His people's release depends. Unlike Aaron's line, He does not need to be replaced: 'because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him,' Hebrews 7:24-25. The release He gives is not until the next high priest; it is forever.

The chapter's refusal of ransom sharpens the gospel. Verse 31 forbids a ransom for a murderer, because a life must answer for a life. Psalm 49:7-8 adds that no one can pay God a ransom for his brother. Yet Jesus says that the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The gospel does not bribe justice. It satisfies it, for God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26.

There is also a striking scene in the Gospels and Acts. Those who crucified Jesus were guilty of shedding innocent blood, and Peter says plainly, 'You killed the Author of life,' Acts 3:15. Yet from the cross Jesus prayed, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, and Peter adds, 'I know that you acted in ignorance,' Acts 3:17. Paul says the same of himself, 1 Timothy 1:13. The killers of the Son of God are offered refuge in the very one they killed.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The cities protected only those who killed without intent, while Christ receives even the deliberate sinner who repents. The pattern is real, but the fulfilment is larger than the shadow. Nor should every detail be pressed: the cubits, the pasturelands and the six cities are not coded messages. The link rests on the New Testament's own language of fleeing, refuge and a high priest whose death sets the captive free.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who values human life because it bears His image. The repeated sentence, 'the murderer must surely be put to death,' is not cruelty but a measure of how precious a human life is to Him. Genesis 9:6 gives the reason: 'in His own image God has made mankind.' To kill a person deliberately is to strike at the likeness of God.

He is a God of careful justice. The law distinguishes weapons, motives and circumstances, verses 16 to 23. It requires the congregation to judge, verse 24, and forbids a death sentence on a single witness, verse 30. God does not treat all killing alike, because He sees the heart. His justice is not rough vengeance but truth applied with care.

He is also merciful, and His mercy is practical. He provides six cities, spread across the land so that no one is far from safety, and He extends that protection to foreigners and strangers, verse 15. He does not wait for an unintentional killer to prove his innocence while exposed to rage; He gives him a place to live while the matter is judged. Scripture's picture of God as refuge, 'a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress,' Isaiah 25:4, is grounded in institutions like this.

The chapter holds justice and mercy together without letting either swallow the other. There is no ransom for murder, verse 31, and no early release for the manslayer, verse 32. Mercy never becomes a loophole, and justice never becomes a weapon for the angry. The cross is where these finally meet, where God shows 'His righteousness' by being 'just' and also the one who justifies, Romans 3:26.

Most of all, the chapter reveals a God who dwells among His people and is holy. 'I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites,' verse 34. His presence is the reason the land must be kept clean. Bloodshed is not only a social wrong but an offence to the God whose tent stands in the midst of the camp. For worship this means that treating our neighbour's life with reverence is part of honouring God, and that when we are guilty we have somewhere to run: 'You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust,' Psalm 91:2.

crossReferences.note: God demands an accounting for every human life and declares that whoever sheds human blood will have his own blood shed, 'for in His own image God has made mankind.' Numbers 35 applies this foundation in detail, which is why the law refuses ransom for a murderer yet takes great care not to execute the innocent.

The first statement of the principle: the one who kills deliberately must die, but for one who 'did not lie in wait,' God promises 'a place where he may flee.' Numbers 35 fulfils that promise by naming six cities, and it keeps the warning that even the altar gives no shelter to a murderer.

Moses repeats the law of refuge before the crossing, adding that roads must be built so the manslayer can reach a city, and that more cities should be added if the land expands. The concern is that the avenger might overtake a man 'in a rage' and kill someone who did not deserve to die.

The cities of refuge are named and set apart: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron west of the Jordan, and Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead and Golan to the east. Joshua adds that the manslayer states his case to the elders at the city gate, showing how the procedure of Numbers 35:24-25 worked in practice.

The total of forty-eight Levitical cities 'together with their pasturelands' matches exactly the number commanded in Numbers 35:7. The Levites, who had no tribal territory, were settled throughout Israel just as God had directed on the plains of Moab.

When a body is found and the killer is unknown, the elders of the nearest town must offer a heifer and pray, 'do not hold the shedding of innocent blood against them.' The passage applies the principle of Numbers 35:33, that unanswered blood lies on the land and must be dealt with before God.

The woman of Tekoa begs David to restrain 'the avenger of blood from increasing the devastation' of her family. Her story shows the avenger was still a real force in Israel's life under the monarchy, and why the protections of Numbers 35 mattered to ordinary families.

The psalmist confesses that Israel 'shed innocent blood' in child sacrifice, 'and the land was polluted with blood.' It is the exact danger Numbers 35:33 warned against, and it explains why Scripture treats bloodshed as a cause of exile, not merely a private crime.

Believers 'who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us' hold an anchor that enters behind the curtain, where Jesus has entered as forerunner and 'high priest forever.' Flight, refuge and a high priest come together, echoing the institution of Numbers 35 and pointing to its fulfilment.

Earlier priests were many because death ended their service, but Jesus lives forever and has a permanent priesthood. Under Numbers 35:28 the manslayer's release depended on a high priest's death; in Christ the priest who died now lives, and His people's release is complete and lasting.

Jesus came 'to give His life as a ransom for many.' Numbers 35:31-32 forbids accepting a ransom for a murderer or for an early release. The gospel does not overturn that justice; the ransom God accepts is the life of His own Son, a price no human payment could match.

The sprinkled blood of Jesus 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.' Abel's blood cried out for justice from the ground, the pollution Numbers 35:33 describes. Christ's blood speaks of atonement and reconciliation, answering the cry of shed blood with mercy grounded in justice satisfied.

study.oneStory:
The problem this chapter addresses goes back almost to the beginning. Cain killed Abel, and Abel's blood cried out from the ground, Genesis 4:10. God protected Cain with a mark, Genesis 4:15, but violence spread until the earth was 'full of violence,' Genesis 6:11, and the flood came. Afterward God set the rule that human blood must be answered, Genesis 9:6. Numbers 35 is where that rule takes shape in the life of a nation, joined to a provision of refuge that keeps justice from turning into endless revenge.

The chapter looks forward to Israel's life in the land and warns of what could go wrong. Bloodshed would pollute the land where God dwells. Israel's later history shows the warning coming true, as innocent blood filled Jerusalem and the land cast out its people, 2 Kings 24:3-4. The cities of refuge could shelter an individual from an avenger, but they could not cleanse a nation's guilt.

That is the gap Christ fills. He is the refuge for the guilty, not only for the unintentional, and His death as high priest opens the way home. His blood speaks a better word than Abel's, Hebrews 12:24. In Him, God's image bearers who have hated and harmed can be forgiven without justice being mocked, because God acts 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26.

The story ends where every cry for blood is finally answered. The martyrs ask, 'How long... until You avenge our blood?' Revelation 6:10, and God does avenge them, Revelation 19:2. In the new creation, murderers remain outside, Revelation 22:15, while all who have fled to the Lamb live in a city where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3, and where there is no more death. The land will never again be polluted, because the One who dwells there has made His people clean.

quiz.q: How many cities in total were given to the Levites, and how many of those were cities of refuge?

options.text: Forty-eight cities total, six of them cities of refuge.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 state both numbers exactly.

options.text: Twelve cities total, all of them cities of refuge.
options.note: The text specifies forty-eight total cities, with only six designated specifically as refuge cities.

options.text: Six cities total, given entirely as refuge cities.
options.note: Six is the correct number of refuge cities specifically, but the Levites received forty-two additional cities beyond these six.

options.text: No specific numbers are given.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 state precise numbers.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the cities of refuge, according to verses 11 to 12?

options.text: To protect a person who killed someone unintentionally from the avenger of blood until a fair trial.
options.note: Verses 11 to 12 state this purpose exactly.

options.text: To provide permanent housing for retired priests.
options.note: Their stated purpose is protection for the unintentional killer, not priestly retirement housing.

options.text: To shelter deliberate murderers from any punishment at all.
options.note: The text specifically distinguishes unintentional killing from murder, and deliberate murderers received no such protection.

options.text: No purpose is given for these cities.
options.note: Verses 11 to 12 state the purpose clearly.

quiz.q: What determined how long the manslayer had to remain within the city of refuge, according to verses 25 and 28?

options.text: He had to remain until the death of the high priest.
options.note: Both verses state this condition directly.

options.text: He had to remain for exactly one full year.
options.note: The text ties his release to the high priest's death, not a fixed one-year term.

options.text: He could leave at any time once the victim's family agreed.
options.note: The text specifies no such family-based release; it is tied strictly to the high priest's death.

options.text: No release condition is mentioned.
options.note: Both verses state the condition explicitly.

quiz.q: What happened if the manslayer left the boundaries of his city of refuge before the high priest's death, according to verses 26 to 27?

options.text: If the avenger of blood found and killed him outside the city, the avenger would not be guilty of bloodshed.
options.note: Verses 26 to 27 state this exact consequence.

options.text: He would simply be escorted back to the city with no other consequence.
options.note: The text specifies real danger and legal consequence if he left the protected boundary, not a simple, safe escort back.

options.text: He would automatically be granted permanent freedom.
options.note: Leaving the city's protection actually placed him at risk, not granted him freedom.

options.text: No consequence for leaving the city is mentioned.
options.note: Verses 26 to 27 describe the consequence in detail.

quiz.q: According to verse 31, could a murderer pay a ransom to avoid the death penalty?

options.text: No, a ransom was explicitly forbidden for a murderer who deserved to die.
options.note: Verse 31 states this prohibition directly.

options.text: Yes, if the victim's family agreed to accept payment.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids any ransom for a convicted murderer, regardless of family agreement.

options.text: Yes, but only if the murderer was wealthy enough.
options.note: No such wealth-based exception exists; the prohibition applies without exception.

options.text: No mention of ransom is made in this chapter.
options.note: Verse 31 addresses ransom explicitly.

questions: The cities of refuge offered real safety, but only for those who fled to them honestly seeking protection. Where in your life do you need to actively run toward the safety God offers rather than passively hoping for protection?

The manslayer's freedom depended entirely on someone else's death, the high priest's, not on his own effort or the passage of time alone. How does resting in what Christ has already accomplished, rather than your own effort, change how you approach guilt or fear of judgment?

This law refused to let murder go unpunished for any price, yet provided genuine mercy for the truly unintentional. Where do you need to hold together taking sin seriously and still extending real mercy to those who have genuinely failed without malicious intent?
The land itself was said to be polluted by unaddressed bloodguilt. Where might unresolved wrongdoing be quietly affecting more of your life or community than you realize?

Six cities meant no Israelite was ever far from a place of refuge. How does knowing that Christ, our refuge, is always near and always accessible change how quickly you turn to Him in a moment of guilt or fear?

translationNotes.note: The two measurements given for Levitical pastureland, a thousand cubits in verse 4 and two thousand cubits in verse 5, are usually harmonized as describing an inner wall boundary and an outer field boundary respectively, rather than a contradiction in the text.

Avenger of blood renders go'el hadam, using the same Hebrew root, go'el, elsewhere translated kinsman-redeemer, showing that both vengeance for the slain and redemption of the lost were understood in ancient Israel as responsibilities carried within the family line.

No atonement can be made for the land on which blood is shed, except by the blood of the one who shed it reflects the seriousness with which the Torah treats bloodguilt as a real defilement of the land itself, not merely a matter between individuals.
